Alexander Downer's now-famous cable helped trigger an FBI counter-intelligence probe into Trump's 2016 campaign "on the thinnest of suspicions".

Jacob Greber

Dec 10, 2019

Washington | It was the paragraph that set off a thundering judicial and political storm that continues to hover over US presidential politics.

Just 34 words long, the key element of former London High Commissioner Alexander Downer's cable to Canberra would become the main trigger for the FBI's controversial counter-intelligence operation into Donald Trump's 2016 campaign.

Alexander Downer's "suggestion of a suggestion" set of a firestorm inside the FBI, according to a long-anticipated US watchdog report. Getty Images

While Mr Downer's unwitting role in unleashing what ultimately turned into Robert Mueller's traumatic two-year Russia probe has been known about for a while, a long-anticipated watchdog's report released in Washington on Monday (Tuesday AEDT) has given fresh support to what Mr Trump and his supporters have been saying all along: that the FBI's so-called Crossfire Hurricane probe was set off by a hair trigger.

Inspector general Michael Horowitz's 434-page report finds there was no evidence of political bias within the bureau's actions, but that the FBI was guilty of sloppy mistakes in its handling of wire-tap applications at the centre of the probe.

"The inspector general’s report now makes clear that the FBI launched an intrusive investigation of a US presidential campaign on the thinnest of suspicions that, in my view, were insufficient to justify the steps taken," said William Barr, the Attorney General.

"It is also clear that, from its inception, the evidence produced by the investigation was consistently exculpatory," he added. "Nevertheless, the investigation and surveillance was pushed forward for the duration of the campaign and deep into President Trump’s administration."

Mr Trump also seized on the report, saying the FBI's efforts amounted to an "attempted overthrow" of the government.

"They had nothing. It was concocted. It's probably something that's never happened in the history of our country," he said at a White House meeting.

Democrats equally claimed vindication, with senior Senator Richard Blumenthal saying Mr Horowitz had "completely demolished" Republican claims about the origins of the FBI probe.

According to Mr Downer, George Papadopoulos indicated knowledge of a Russian "dirt" file on then Democrat candidate Hillary Clinton. AP

"Clearly, there was a legitimate, factual basis; in fact the FBI had a moral imperative to begin this investigation,” Senator Blumenthal said.

Mr Downer - who's identity is thinly concealed throughout the report as a "friendly foreign government", or "FFG", source - clocks up no fewer than 144 mentions in the Horowitz report,

Time and time again the report underscores how Mr Downer's account of a May, 2016, meeting he had with lowly Trump campaign aide George Papadopoulos in a London bar became the critical catalyst for the FBI's counter-intelligence investigation into four people associated with the then-candidate, Mr Trump.

During their talk, according to Mr Downer, Mr Papadopoulos indicated knowledge of a Russian "dirt" file on then Democrat candidate Hillary Clinton.

While Mr Downer relayed a description of that conversation at the time to Canberra, he only alerted his US counterparts in London in late July, 2016, four days after a massive WikiLeaks release of hacked Democratic National Committee emails.

The Horowitz report for the first time reveals a read-out of Mr Downer's description to American investigators - something Australian officials have been resisting until recently for fear it would undermine the free flow of intelligence-sharing between so-called "Five Eyes" partners.

Andrew McCabe told the Horowitz inquiry the "decision to open the case was unanimous". AP

Mr Downer stated that Mr Papadopoulos "suggested the Trump team had received some kind of suggestion from Russia that it could assist this process with the anonymous release of information during the campaign that would be damaging to Mrs Clinton [and President Obama]", according to Monday's report.

The former ambassador added: "It was unclear whether he or the Russians were referring to material acquired publicly of (sic) through other means. It was also unclear how Mr Trump's team reacted to the offer.

"We note the Trump team's reaction could, in the end, have little bearing of what Russia decides to do, with or without Mr Trump's cooperation."

Once those words reached the FBI, they set off a dramatic escalation inside the bureau that led to the politically-charged Russia investigation.

Andrew McCabe, then deputy director of the FBI, told the Horowitz inquiry the "decision to open the case was unanimous".

"McCabe said the FBI viewed the FFG [Downer] information in the context of Russian attempts to interfere with the 2016 US elections in the years and months prior, as well as the FBI's ongoing investigation into the DNC hack by a Russian intelligence service," the report states.

When the FBI received Mr Downer's information it was a "tipping point" in terms of opening a counter-intelligence investigation, Mr McCabe said, according to the report.

"Now the FBI had received an allegation from a trusted partner that there had been some sort of contact between the Russians and the Trump campaign."

According to David Laufman, who was the FBI's then chief of the national security division's counterintelligence and export section, his impression was that Mr Downer's information had "raised obvious alarm bells in the FBI" and had "resonated" with him.

He told the inquiry that it would have been "a dereliction of duty and responsibility of the highest order not to commit the appropriate resources as urgently as possible to run these facts to the ground, and find out what was going on".
